html:
A Roman aqueduct bridge over the river Gardon in southern France, built in the 1st century CE to carry water to the Roman colony of Nemausus, now Nîmes. It is one of the best preserved works of Roman engineering.

It has three tiers of arches, rising about 49 metres, the highest of any Roman aqueduct bridge. The two lower tiers are built of huge stone blocks fitted without mortar. The water channel runs along the top.

The bridge is a small part of an aqueduct about 50 km long, from springs near Uzès to Nîmes. The whole channel drops only about 12 metres over that length, a sign of how precisely Roman aqueduct builders could survey. Water flowed until the early Middle Ages, when lack of upkeep let lime deposits block the channel.

Later the bridge was used as a road, and in 1743 a new road bridge was built alongside. It lies in what had been Gallia Narbonensis, the oldest Roman province in Gaul. Like the Aqueduct of Segovia, it is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a symbol of the Roman Empire.
sum: A Roman aqueduct bridge over the river Gardon in southern France, built in the 1st century CE to carry water to the Roman colony of Nemausus, now Nîmes. It is one of the best preserved works of Roman engineering.
